questions.question: What is a software inspection and how does it differ from testing in terms of execution requirements?

options.A: It is a dynamic technique that requires running the software to find defects.
options.B: It is a static technique that does not require executing the software.
options.C: It is a form of debugging performed after testing failures are identified.
options.D: It is an automated tool that generates test cases from source code.

questions.explanation:
Software inspections are described as “static” V&V techniques where you don’t need to execute the software to verify it. [Page 38]

---

questions.question: According to the context, which artifacts can be examined during a software inspection?

options.B: Requirements, design models, source code, and proposed system tests.

questions.explanation:
Inspections can analyze and check system requirements, design models, program source code, and even proposed system tests. [Page 38]

---

questions.question: Why might an organization choose inspections over testing for detecting interface errors?

options.A: Inspections can automatically fix the detected errors.
options.B: Inspections can concentrate on component interfaces without needing to run the software.
options.C: Inspections are cheaper because they replace all testing activities.
options.D: Inspections guarantee that no runtime errors will ever occur.

questions.explanation:
The context states that inspections can be better for looking for interface errors because they can concentrate on component interfaces and assumed behavior during the inspection process. [Page 48]

---

questions.question: What advantage of software inspections over testing is explicitly mentioned in the material?

options.B: Inspections can be performed earlier in the development lifecycle.
options.C: Inspections require less specialized knowledge than testing.
options.D: Inspections eliminate the need for any subsequent testing.

questions.explanation:
The text lists three advantages of inspections over testing, one of which is that they can be applied at earlier stages of the process. [Page 38]

---

questions.question: In the Cleanroom process, what proportion of defects is claimed to be discoverable through program inspections?
questions.explanation:
The Cleanroom process claims that more than 90 % of defects can be discovered in program inspections. [Page 39]

---

questions.question: How do inspections contribute to verification according to the provided text?

options.A: By executing the software with a full set of test cases.
options.B: By checking that the software meets its stated functional and non‑functional requirements without running it.
options.C: By measuring performance metrics during runtime.
options.D: By collecting user feedback after deployment.

questions.explanation:
Verification is defined as checking that software meets its requirements, and inspections are a static method to perform that checking without execution. [Page 37, Page 38]

---

questions.question: Which statement best captures the role of knowledge about the application domain during an inspection?

options.A: It is unnecessary because inspections only focus on syntax errors.
options.B: It helps the inspector discover errors in requirements, design, or code.
options.C: It replaces the need for any formal inspection checklist.
options.D: It is only relevant when inspecting user interface mock‑ups.

questions.explanation:
When inspecting a system, you use knowledge of the system, its application domain, and the programming or modeling language to discover errors. [Page 38]

---

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of fault that testing aims to uncover, as described in the context?
questions.explanation:
Testing seeks to find undesirable system behavior such as crashes, unwanted interactions, incorrect computations, and data corruption, but not documentation formatting issues. [Page 36]

---

questions.question: How does the inspection process relate to the overall verification and validation (V&V) activities?

options.A: Inspections are the only V&V activity required before release.
options.B: Inspections and testing support V&V at different stages of the software process.
options.C: Inspections replace validation because they verify user expectations.
options.D: Inspections are performed after all testing is completed.

questions.explanation:
The text notes that inspections and testing support V&V at different stages, indicating complementary roles. [Page 38]

---

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why inspections are classified as “static” techniques?

options.A: They involve running the software with static input data.
options.B: They analyze software artifacts without executing the program.
options.C: They use static code analysis tools that automatically modify code.
options.D: They focus only on static variables in the source code.

questions.explanation: Inspections are described as static V&V techniques where you do not need to execute the software to verify it. [Page 38]
